evidence.label: Monochromatic finite sums and products in the positive integers

headline: However whole numbers are colored, some set of each size has its sums and products in one color, the paper claims.
scope: The result covers every coloring of the positive integers with finitely many colors, and finite sets of any prescribed size.
plain: Color every positive whole number with one of a few colors. Hindman conjectured that, for any size k, some k numbers have all their subset sums and subset products in a single color. This paper claims to prove that conjecture. The sets are finite; Hindman had shown that infinite versions can fail. No Lean formalization is listed.
doesNot: This does not give an infinite set with this property; Hindman showed in 1980 that such sets need not exist.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.firstStepBy: Neil Hindman, who posed the finite conjecture
scorecard.significanceWhy: If the proof holds, it settles a decades-old conjecture that mixes addition and multiplication in Ramsey theory.

explanation:
Color each positive whole number red or blue by one rule. Write it in binary. If it has an even number of binary digits, color it red; if odd, blue. So 3, written 11, is red. So is 12, written 1100.

Now look for a set whose sums and products all share one color. Take {3, 11}. The sums are 3, 11 and 14. The products are 3, 11 and 33. All four numbers have an even number of binary digits, so all are red. Try three numbers: {3, 12, 228}. Their seven subset sums and seven subset products give 11 different numbers. Every one of them is red.

Hindman's conjecture says this always works[1]. Pick any number of colors, any coloring and any size k. Then some k-element set has all its nonempty subset sums and subset products in one color[1]. A subset sum adds some of the numbers, each used at most once. A subset product multiplies them the same way.

Sums alone and products alone were handled long ago. Schur's theorem, from 1916, finds x, y and x + y in one color[2]. The Folkman–Rado–Sanders theorem extends this to all subset sums of large finite sets[3]. Recoloring each n by the color of 2ⁿ turns sum results into product results[4]. Mixing both is different. In 1980 Hindman built a coloring with no infinite set whose terms, pairwise sums and pairwise products share a color[5]. His finite conjecture asks only for large finite sets[6].

Partial results came in steps. Moreira proved in 2017 that x, x + y and xy can share a color, for any finite coloring[7]. Over the rational numbers, which include fractions, Bowen and Sabok found x, y, x + y and xy in one color[8]. Alweiss then proved the full sums-and-products theorem over the rationals[9].

This paper claims to prove the conjecture for the positive integers[10]. It also claims the numbers can be spread so far apart that no two expressions collide, apart from the numbers themselves[11]. Then a k-element set gives 2(2ᵏ − 1) − k different same-colored numbers[12]. For k = 3 that is 11, as in the example.

The obstacle is moving from fractions to whole numbers. Clearing denominators means multiplying everything by one common number. That scales a sum by one power of it, but a product of j entries by its j-th power[13]. A coloring need not respect those different changes[13]. The new work keeps control of the additive shifts while protecting the product colors[14]. It does this by building bounded predictions for where each color appears, then picking scales that keep those predictions positive at the needed sums.

How sure is this? No Lean formalization is listed for this paper in the openai/math release. So no computer proof checker has checked it. No specialist review has been published.
hypeCheck: Major only if the proof holds. It gives finite sets of every size, not infinite ones. No Lean formalization is listed and no specialist review is published.

glossary.meaning: A rule that gives each positive integer one of finitely many labels, called colors.
The sum of a nonempty selection of the set's numbers, each used at most once.
The product of a nonempty selection of the set's numbers, each used at most once.
The study of patterns that must appear in one color, however a large structure is colored.
Numbers that can be written as fractions of whole numbers.

claims.text: For every finite coloring and every k, some k-element set has all nonempty subset sums and products in one color.
claims.sourceLine: for every finite coloring of the positive integers and every positive integer
claims.sourceQuote: We prove Hindman's finite sums and products conjecture: for every finite coloring of the positive integers and every positive integer $k$, there is a $k$-element set whose nonempty subset sums and nonempty subset products all have the same color.
